entity.name: Johannes Kepler
entity.description: The astronomer who proved planets move in ellipses, not circles. Kepler discovered three laws of planetary motion that became the foundation for Newton's theory of gravity. A sickly child with weak eyesight who could barely observe the stars he mathematically mastered, he also defended his mother against charges of witchcraft.

story.name: Johannes Kepler
story.description: A nearly blind astronomer inherits Tycho Brahe's data in Prague, proves planets orbit in ellipses, defends his mother from witchcraft charges, and dies penniless chasing an unpaid salary. The mathematician who gave Newton the laws to explain.

moments.name: Johannes Kepler Is Born in the Free Imperial City of Weil der Stadt
moments.subtitle: A sickly, premature child who would rewrite the laws of the heavens
moments.description: On 27 December 1571, Johannes Kepler was born in the Free Imperial City of Weil der Stadt in the Duchy of Wurttemberg. Born prematurely to a mercenary father who soon abandoned the family and a mother later accused of witchcraft, Kepler was weak and sickly throughout childhood. Smallpox left him with crippled hands and weak vision, severely limiting his ability to make astronomical observations. Yet at age six, his mother took him to a hilltop to watch the Great Comet of 1577, sparking a lifelong passion for the heavens he could barely see. Kepler would go on to discover the laws governing planetary motion.

moments.name: Kepler Meets Tycho Brahe and Gains Access to the Best Star Data on Earth
moments.subtitle: Two rival astronomers form the most productive partnership in science history
moments.description: On 4 February 1600, Johannes Kepler arrived at Benatky nad Jizerou near Prague to meet the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe, who possessed the most accurate astronomical observations ever recorded. Brahe guarded his data jealously but was impressed by Kepler's theoretical brilliance and gradually granted access. Their collaboration was tense and brief, as Brahe died in October 1601, but Kepler inherited the precious Mars observations. Using Brahe's data, Kepler would spend years proving that Mars orbited the Sun in an ellipse, overthrowing 2,000 years of circular-orbit astronomy.

moments.name: Kepler Publishes Astronomia Nova, Proving Planets Orbit in Ellipses
moments.subtitle: Two thousand years of circular-orbit astronomy overturned by one book
moments.description: In 1609, Johannes Kepler published Astronomia Nova while serving as Imperial Mathematician in Prague. The book contained his first two laws of planetary motion: that planets orbit the Sun in ellipses with the Sun at one focus, and that a line from planet to Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times. The breakthrough came after years of failed attempts to fit Mars's orbit into a circle using Tycho Brahe's precise data. Kepler found that an elliptical orbit fit the data with stunning accuracy. These laws demolished the ancient assumption of circular planetary motion and laid the mathematical groundwork for Newton's gravitational theory.

moments.name: Kepler Discovers His Third Law of Planetary Motion in Linz
moments.subtitle: The mathematical harmony linking every planet's orbit to its distance from the Sun
moments.description: On 15 May 1618, while living in Linz, Austria, Johannes Kepler discovered his third law of planetary motion: that the square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its average distance from the Sun. He published the finding in Harmonice Mundi (Harmony of the World) in 1619. Kepler had been searching for mathematical harmony in the cosmos for over two decades, convinced that God had designed the universe according to geometric principles. This third law completed the trio of laws that Isaac Newton would later use to derive the universal law of gravitation.

moments.name: Kepler Dies Penniless in Regensburg While Chasing Unpaid Salary
moments.subtitle: The man who mapped the heavens could never secure his own finances
moments.description: On 15 November 1630, Johannes Kepler died in Regensburg, Bavaria, at age 58. He had traveled there to collect 12,000 florins in unpaid salary owed to him by the Imperial treasury. Kepler had spent his final years in financial hardship, moving between cities as religious wars disrupted his employment. His grave in the St. Peter's churchyard was destroyed when the Swedish army took Regensburg during the Thirty Years' War just two years later. The astronomer who discovered the laws governing planetary motion died unable to collect his earthly wages.
